title: CI-only failure: the cause string in a degraded git check-ignore warning
question: Diagnose this CI-only failure, where a test pinned to one cause string in a degraded-scan warning sees a different cause string on the runner than it does locally and on main. Decide whether to re-run it as a flake, loosen or retarget the assertion, or change the code, and say what the code should report. Give your decision and the next steps, including who is affected.

rubric.decision: A real race, not a flake: git check-ignore --stdin outside a work tree exits 128 without reading stdin while spawnSync is still writing, so the parent sees either status 128 or EPIPE depending on platform/load. Fix the cause reporting in code (a non-zero status other than 0/1 wins over the write error; a write error with status 0/1 keeps its own code) and leave the test unchanged; the loud degradation held either way. Not a re-run and not a loosened regex.

keyPoints.text: Rejects "flake" and "wrong expectation": a cause string that varies with platform/load is itself the defect, since an operator has to re-derive the real cause.

Explains the mechanism: in a non-work-tree git exits 128 immediately without consuming stdin while node's spawnSync is still writing the input, so the parent sees either exit status 128 or an EPIPE write error depending on timing/platform.
Identifies the code-order bug: ign.error is checked before ign.status, so a transient write error masks the real exit status; EPIPE after the child has exited carries no extra information.

Fixes it at the cause-reporting site: a non-zero status other than 0/1 wins, but a write error alongside status 0/1 keeps its own code (child answered; output may be truncated; still degraded); adds controls for both orders.
Notes the behaviour under test (degrade loudly, never report a clean scan) held in both cases, so the test should stay unchanged.
Scopes impact: the module ships to consumers so the fix reaches them on re-sync; main is latent rather than red; a race proves nothing by passing.

traps.text: Retargets the regex to accept (EPIPE|git exit 128), hiding the nondeterminism.
Treats EPIPE as a runner-specific environmental artefact and ignores the code path that reports it.
Collapses all write errors into the exit status, which would mislabel truncated output under status 0/1.

controls.gold:
This is a real, nondeterministic defect in the code's cause reporting, not a flake and not a wrong expectation. The test runs extract against a scratch root that is not a git work tree, where `git check-ignore -z --stdin` prints "fatal: not a git repository" and exits 128 immediately, without consuming stdin, while `spawnSync` is still writing the NUL-joined candidate list into the pipe. The parent therefore observes either status 128 (Windows locally) or an `EPIPE` write error (the loaded Linux runner), depending on timing. The code builds the warning with `ign.error ? ign.error.code : git exit ${ign.status}`, so the transient write error is checked first and masks the real exit status; an EPIPE after the child has already exited adds no information. That the cause string depends on platform and load is itself the bug, because an operator would have to re-derive the cause.

Decision on options: do not re-run, and do not loosen the regex to accept both strings, which would hide the nondeterminism. Fix it where the cause is reported: a non-zero status other than 0/1 should win over the write error, while a write error alongside status 0 or 1 keeps its own code, because the child answered and its output may be truncated (still degraded). The test stays unchanged; add controls for both orderings. The behaviour under test, degrading loudly and never reporting a clean scan, held in both cases.

Impact: the module ships to consumers, so the fix reaches them on re-sync; main is latent, not red.

## Decision

Change the code so a non-zero exit status wins over a write error in the degraded-scan cause, keep the test as is, and add both-order controls; do not retry or loosen the assertion.
controls.trap:
This is an environment-specific flake and the test is over-pinned. The scan correctly degraded and loudly said so on both platforms: the warning on the runner reads "could not determine gitignore status (EPIPE) — ownership was NOT verified", which is the same condition as "git exit 128" described by the test. Linux and Windows simply handle a closed pipe differently when git refuses to run in a directory that is not a work tree, and `EPIPE` is the pipe-level symptom of the same failure, so nothing is wrong in `ignoredUntrackedPaths`. The code already returns `degraded: true` with a warning and never claims a clean scan, which is the behaviour the test was written to protect.

The right response is to make the test describe that behaviour rather than one operating system's spelling of it. Retarget the assertion to accept either cause, `/could not determine gitignore status \((EPIPE|git exit 128)\)/`, keep the degraded-line assertions, and re-run the job to confirm it goes green. No change to the module is needed, so nothing changes for consumers either, and the Windows run still exercises the 128 path.

## Decision

Treat it as a runner-specific flake: loosen the regex to accept EPIPE or git exit 128, re-run the full suite, and make no code change.
